newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Beleaguered MacMillan seeks to soothe investors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Beleaguered MacMillan seeks to soothe investors.

text.p: Beleaguered MacMillan Bloedel Ltd., Canada's biggest forestry concern, sought Wednesday to reassure shareholders about its future even as it slashed its quarterly dividend and faced persistent rumors that it may be forced into a restructuring.

MacMillan, a major producer of lumber and paper, has seen its losses mount amid growing pressure from shareholders disappointed with its performance. Analysts have speculated for more than a year that the company may be ripe for a breakup including the sale of its paper business.
Before its annual meeting on Wednesday, MacMillan cut its dividend to C$0.05 a share from C$0.15, a move that will save it about C$50 million ($37 million) a year.
MacMillan said its poor earnings forced the move and Chief Executive Robert Findlay told reporters that losses in the company's packaging business were the primary problem.
MacMillan's stock ended 0.20 lower at 19.10 on the Toronto exhange after the news.

Amid market speculation that MacMillan may divest its paper division, Findlay did little to dispel talk that the unit may be a candidate for sale. While saying there were no changes planned for the operation now, he said merging the business with another paper maker would make sense.

The paper division, which contributes about 14 percent of MacMillan's C$5 billion ($3.7 billion) in sales, "probably should be merged" as Abitibi-Price Inc. recently did with Stone Consolidated Corp, he said.
The logical partner would be Vancouver's Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd., but a deal was unlikely despite years of talks between the two companies, he said.
Findlay said MacMillan had no other potential partners in mind, although it was "always having discussions."

"So sure we would like to grow (the paper business) and we might even merge it...," Findlay said. Asked if Bowater Inc. of the United States might be interested, Findlay said he did not want to comment.

In his speech to shareholders, Findlay laid out MacMillan's strategy including long-term plans for the paper operation. Recent moves have positioned the company for a turnaround when commodity prices improve, he said.

"...This company is well positioned for the future," he said, forecasting that the company's sales will climb to C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) in 1998 from around C$5 billion ($3.7 billion) a year currently.

But he also acknowledged shareholder discontent and the company announced it would appoint Thomas Taylor to its board as a representative of the billionaire Bass brothers of Texas and the Ontario Teachers Plan Board.

Last month, Taylor and Co. of Fort Worth, which invests for the secretive Bass brothers, and the pension fund said they jointly acquired 9.5 percent of MacMillan. The purchase made them the company's biggest shareholders and analysts believe their presence could hasten a restructuring.
Asked if Taylor's group supported MacMillan management and the company's current direction, MacMillan Chairman Robert Haskayne said, "They've obviously got confidence in us for the long term."
Taylor attended the annual meeting, but Findlay told reporters that Taylor did not want to speak to the media. The Bass brothers are known for keeping a low profile.

Noting restructuring steps MacMillan has already taken, Findlay confirmed that MacMillan will sell its loss-making American Cemwood division based in Oregon, which produces synthetic roofing, and Kingcome Navigation, its tugboat operation.

Findlay reiterated calls for relief from regulatory costs at MacMillan's logging operations and said negotiations between British Columbia's forest companies and the provincial government on a scheme were making slow progress.
